summary: Provides a general mechanism for using the header extension feature of RTP, the Real-Time Transport Protocol. It allows a small number of small extensions in each packet, from a large universe of possible extensions with decentralized registration. The extensions in use are signaled when the session is set up. It was replaced by RFC 8285.

plainLanguage.summary: Each package in a video call can carry a small sticker with extra info, like volume level. This describes a tidy way to add several stickers. It was replaced by RFC 8285.

questions: how to add extension to rtp packets
subtitle: A standard way to attach multiple small pieces of extra data to RTP packets.

tldr.problem: RTP packets can carry metadata alongside audio or video, but the original RTP spec only allows one header extension per packet and provides no standard way to identify different extensions, risking collisions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5285 defines two formats (one-byte and two-byte headers) that let an RTP packet carry multiple named extensions, each with a small local identifier. Session setup via SDP signals which extensions are in use, mapping local identifiers to URIs and allowing decentralized registration.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now attach metadata like absolute send time, transport-wide congestion information, or volume levels to RTP packets without formal registration. RFC 8285 later refined and replaced this specification.

today: RFC 5285 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 8285, which provides clarifications and updates to the extension mechanism.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
RTP is the protocol used for real-time audio and video. The original RTP specification (RFC 3550) includes a header extension mechanism, but it has two limitations. First, it allows only one extension per packet. Second, the 16-bit identifiers for extensions have no formal allocation scheme, so different vendors might accidentally use the same number and cause collisions.

RFC 5285 solves both problems. It defines a way to pack multiple small extensions into a single RTP header extension field. It also uses URIs to name extensions and provides an IANA registry for IETF-defined extensions, plus an SDP attribute to signal which extensions a session uses.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP packets can carry extra information, but the old way only allowed one piece of extra info per packet and didn't prevent different apps from using the same label. This RFC lets packets carry several pieces of extra info and gives each a proper name.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
The extension mechanism is meant for optional metadata that a receiver can safely ignore without breaking the stream. Examples include absolute send time, audio volume, or transport congestion feedback. The extensions should not be bundled into the media payload itself, as that would require knowing the metadata at encoding time and might affect bandwidth calculations.

Each extension in a packet has a local identifier (ID) and a length. The local IDs are small (1-14 for the one-byte form, 1-255 for the two-byte form) and are mapped to larger URIs out-of-band via SDP. This allows a small header while supporting a huge namespace of possible extensions.

Extensions should only be present in packets where they are needed, and extensions MUST only be used for data that can be safely ignored. They MUST NOT change the form or nature of the packet in a way incompatible with how the stream is signaled.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra info is like a note you can add to a package—it helps explain what's inside, but if someone ignores the note, the package still works. Each note gets a short nickname in this package and a full name elsewhere.

sections.title: The Two Header Formats
sections.content:
RFC 5285 defines two formats, and a stream must use only one consistently. The one-byte header form uses a magic 16-bit value 0xBEDE and packs each extension as: one byte containing a 4-bit ID (range 1-14) and a 4-bit length field. The length field stores the number of data bytes minus one, allowing 1-16 bytes of data per extension. ID 15 is reserved for future use and signals the end of extensions.

The two-byte header form uses a magic value of 0x100 with 4 application-defined bits. Each extension uses two bytes: a full byte for the ID (range 1-255) and a full byte for the length (0-255 bytes of data). ID 256 (encoded in the application bits) is also defined.

Both formats support padding bytes (value 0) for alignment. Padding bytes are ignored during parsing.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to write the sticker: one for short stickers (one byte with a 4-bit label and 4-bit size), and one for longer stickers (two bytes with an 8-bit label and 8-bit size). You pick one way and stick with it for the whole call.

sections.title: SDP Signaling
sections.content:
The extensions in use during a session are negotiated via SDP (Session Description Protocol), typically in a SIP offer/answer exchange. Each extension is named by a URI, which must be absolute and precisely identify the extension. For IETF RFCs, the URI should start with urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext: followed by a descriptive name. Other organizations may use HTTP URIs with a date stamp (mmyyyy) indicating when the extension was defined.

The SDP attribute a=extmap:<id> <URI> maps a local identifier to an extension URI. The ID must be in the valid range for the chosen header format. Each extension URI can appear at most once per media stream, though the same extension may be used across multiple streams with different IDs.

Direction attributes (sendonly, recvonly, sendrecv, inactive) can be appended to control in which direction an extension flows. In offer/answer negotiation, parties can modify direction qualifiers, add or remove extensions, or remap IDs from the negotiation range (4096-4351) to the valid range.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the call starts, both sides agree on which stickers will be used and what each number means. They use names like "urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:absolute-send-time" so there's no confusion.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
A simple example: a=extmap:1 http://example.com/082005/ext.htm#ttime maps local ID 1 to that URI. In the RTP packet, ID 1 carries data for that extension.

A more complex example with direction: a=extmap:2/sendrecv http://example.com/082005/ext.htm#xmeta maps ID 2 to that extension and indicates both sides can send and receive it.

During offer/answer, if a party wants to offer mutually exclusive alternatives (e.g., two ways to encode GPS data), it can use IDs in the range 4096-4351. The answerer selects the desired alternative and remaps it to a free ID in the valid range.
sections.plainLanguage: An example might be: "sticker 1 means absolute-send-time" and "sticker 2 means volume-level, both directions." If offering multiple choices, you use higher numbers, and the answerer picks one and gives it a normal number.

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Local identifier of the extension, range 1-14.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Extension data length minus one; 0-15 means 1-16 bytes.
